content.title: Eliminating Redundant Words and Information
content.overview: Redundancy occurs when two or more words in a sentence repeat the same meaning. On the ACT, the most effective writing is concise. This lesson teaches you to identify overlapping word pairs and select the shortest phrasing that preserves the necessary detail and tone.
learning_objectives: Identify redundant word pairs and phrases that repeat the same idea.
Apply the Redundancy Pair-Trim strategy to remove unnecessary repetition.
Distinguish between concise phrasing and phrasing that loses essential meaning or nuance.

sections.title: Recognizing Redundancy
sections.content: Redundancy is the use of two words or phrases next to each other that convey the same idea. Common examples include 'added bonus' (a bonus is already something added), 'past history' (history is by definition in the past), and 'each and every' (both words signal individuality). When you see two adjacent words that seem to state the same thing, you have triggered a redundancy check.

sections.title: The Redundancy Pair-Trim Strategy
sections.content: To eliminate redundancy, follow these steps: 1. Underline the overlapping words or phrases. 2. Identify the core word that carries the intended idea. 3. Choose the shortest option that preserves the original meaning and necessary detail. 4. Read the sentence back to ensure the tone and emphasis remain intact. Remember: shorter is usually better, but only if the meaning is not compromised.

sections.title: Conciseness vs. Omission
sections.content: A common trap on the ACT is choosing an option that is short but removes a specific detail or formal nuance required by the context. While 'different speakers' is shorter than 'a diverse array of speakers,' the latter conveys a specific sense of variety and professional tone that 'different' lacks. Always ensure your choice retains the 'flavor' of the original sentence while cutting the 'fat' of the repetition.

worked_examples.question:
The archaeological team discovered [an ancient, old artifact] buried deep within the desert sands. 

Which choice best eliminates redundancy?
A. NO CHANGE
B. an old artifact
C. an ancient artifact
D. an ancient, old, and aged artifact
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the overlap. 'Ancient' and 'old' both describe the age of the object. Step 2: Determine the core word. 'Ancient' is more precise for an archaeological context than 'old.' Step 3: Select the shortest option that keeps the detail. Choice C ('an ancient artifact') removes the repetition while keeping the specific detail. Choice B is also concise but less precise. Choice C is the best fit.

worked_examples.question:
The committee members [collaborated together on] the new environmental policy. 

Which choice best eliminates redundancy?
A. NO CHANGE
B. collaborated on
C. worked together in collaboration on
D. joined together to collaborate on
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the overlap. 'Collaborated' means to work together, so 'together' is redundant. Step 2: Select the shortest option. Choice B ('collaborated on') removes the redundant word 'together' and is the most direct phrasing. Choices C and D actually add more redundant words.

common_mistakes: Choosing the shortest answer even if it changes the meaning of the sentence.
Failing to recognize that a single word can encompass the meaning of a two-word phrase (e.g., 'sum total').
Ignoring the tone of the passage; sometimes a slightly longer phrase is needed to maintain a formal or technical style.
exam_tips: If you see 'DELETE the underlined portion' as an option, check for redundancy first; it is often the correct answer if the information is repeated elsewhere.
Watch out for 'time' redundancy, such as 'currently... at this moment' or 'annually... every year.'
When two options seem grammatically correct, the shorter one is almost always the right answer on the ACT.
content.recap: Redundancy clutters writing. To succeed on the ACT, identify words that repeat the same meaning, select the most precise core word, and choose the shortest phrasing that maintains the original intent and tone.

knowledge_claims.content: Redundancy is the use of two or more words or phrases that repeat the same meaning within a sentence.
A redundancy check is triggered when two adjacent words or phrases, such as 'each and every,' convey the same idea.
The first step in the Redundancy Pair-Trim strategy is to underline the overlapping words or phrases to identify the repetition.
When eliminating redundancy, the goal is to choose the shortest option that preserves the original meaning and necessary detail.
After replacing a redundant pair, the final check is to read the sentence aloud to ensure the original meaning and required emphasis are preserved.
It is a mistake to choose a shorter phrasing if it removes a specific nuance or formal tone intended by the original text.
Phrases like 'past history' and 'added bonus' are redundant because the modifier is already implied by the definition of the noun.
The phrase 'a diverse array of speakers' is superior to 'different speakers' if the context requires a formal tone and specific emphasis on variety.
In the phrase 'collaborated together,' the word 'together' should be removed because 'collaborated' already means working with others.
Time-based redundancy often involves pairing an adverb like 'annually' with a phrase like 'each year' or 'every year.'
On the ACT English section, if two options are both grammatically correct, the more concise option is generally preferred.
When evaluating redundancy, identify the 'core word' that carries the essential meaning and discard the duplicate word.

items.stem:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 1: The Clock Above Alder Street
[1] After three months of fundraising [[a neighborhood restoration crew began]] to repair the brass clock above Alder Street Market. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a market hall built in 1911, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] wear marks showed that an earlier repairer had reversed two nearly identical wheels. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because replacement parts would have erased those clues. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the crew cleaned and reused the original wheels. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the clock kept accurate time through a week of rain. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.]]

Which choice most effectively replaces the wording marked [7]?
items.explanation: 'Essential' alone expresses the idea precisely and concisely.

items.stem:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 2: Counting After Dark
[1] After several cloudy evenings [[a coastal ecology class began]] to count juvenile crabs in tide pools after sunset. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a protected inlet beside the school, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] the smallest crabs appeared most often under flat stones near eelgrass. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because bright white light changed the animals’ movement. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the class switched to dim red lamps and repeated the first survey. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the second set of counts was more consistent. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the revised method gave park staff a dependable baseline for future surveys.]]

Which choice most effectively replaces the wording marked [7]?
items.explanation: 'Essential' alone expresses the idea precisely and concisely.
